name: Face tanning for 'glow'

lead: People darken facial skin to look healthier or hide redness, using sun or tanning beds, or sunless products such as DHA self-tanners and bronzers.
Sunless products fade over days. Studies specifically testing face tanning for glow were not found.

paras: DHA reacts with amino acids in the skin's dead outer layer to produce a brown colour without UV. Bronzers are surface pigments that wash off.
UV tanning is associated with skin cancer risk. Sunless products can cause contact dermatitis, are not approved for eyes, lips or inhalation, and give no UV protection.

lead: Face tanning for 'glow' means darkening or warming the facial skin tone, either through sun or tanning-bed exposure or through sunless products such as self-tanners and bronzers, with the aim of looking healthier or masking redness.

Sunless methods include DHA-based self-tanners and temporary bronzers. Wikipedia describes DHA as reacting with amino acids in the outer dead skin layer, with colour fading over about 3 to 10 days, and says a sunless tan does not protect against UV.[1] Patent filings describe cosmetic compositions for sunless tanning or imparting glow.[2][3]

paras: DHA was noticed to stain skin brown in the 1950s by Eva Wittgenstein; Man-Tan (1959) and Coppertone's QT (1960) were early products, and their orange tone harmed the category's image. Spray-tan booths expanded the market from the late 1990s.[1]

Bronzers are temporary products that wash off and are used for one-day colour or to complement a DHA tan.[1] Patent documents describe compositions in which a tanning agent is combined with a cationic copolymer to intensify colour and reduce streaking.[2][3]

Wikipedia reports the FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around eyes, lips, mucous membranes or for inhalation. A 2007 study found more free radicals formed after sun exposure in DHA-treated skin, and a 2010 European scientific committee opinion concluded DHA spray tanning posed no risk, a conclusion criticised by some specialists. DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis in some people.[1]
The article reports that UV tanning is linked to skin cancer risk and that unlicensed melanotan injections have been subject to health agency warnings since 2007.[1]

No studies found on the effect of face tanning on perceived glow or redness masking in the sources reviewed. Wikipedia cites a 2011 study in which a carotenoid-based golden skin tone was rated more attractive and healthy-looking than a suntan.[1]

timeline.event: Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner.[1]
